normalized.governing_thought: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing, not hours: with store exits, the margin reaches 3.0% by FY2028
executive_summary: Promotions, shrink and e-commerce caused 87% of the margin fall; wages only 13% – Operating income fell 68% while sales grew 6%; the target needs $29.8M more a year (p. 5–7)
Move store hours instead of cutting them, and exit the nine loss-making stores – An 8% cut could lose $10.0M of its $14.5M saving to shrink; moving hours saves $4.2M (p. 9–16)
Return promotions to the FY2023 mix outside ValuMart areas, and grow private label – Promotion mix caused over two-thirds of the gross-margin fall; the reset adds $9.9M (p. 18–24)
Keep e-commerce but charge for delivery, which wins back $2.8M of a $10.4M loss – Each home delivery loses about $12; the fee test lost only 2% of e-commerce sales (p. 26–31)

First: promotions, delivery fees and store hours, which need no capital – Five moves add $27.4M a year and lift the margin to 3.0% by FY2028 – Together the first three cover the FY2026 covenant need; $6.5M of reserves cover most wage risk (p. 33–41)

slides.title: Reversing the margin decline
Key questions

claims.claim: How can Harlow lift its operating margin from 1.0% in FY2025 to at least 3.0% by FY2028, within $25M of one-time cost and the $20M FY2026 covenant, and which actions should come first?
evidence: Decision maker: CEO, seeking board approval of the margin plan and its first actions

Success criteria: Operating margin of at least 3.0% by FY2028; Operating income of at least $20M in FY2026 (lender covenant); At most $25M of one-time cost or capital over FY2026–FY2028; No closure of a store with a lease beyond 2027 without a board vote; delivery kept in some form
Timing: Board meeting, February 2027
Out of scope: Closing delivery (owners' commitment); Refinancing the covenant; Spending beyond the $25M budget

slides.title: Contents
Promotions, shrink and e-commerce explain 87% of the margin decline, wages only 13%

claims.claim: 87% of the 2.35 percentage-point fall came from promotion mix, shrink and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart: FY2023 3.37%; Promotion mix −0.70 pp; Shrink −0.50 pp; Private label +0.18 pp; E-commerce fulfillment −0.84 pp; Store labor −0.30 pp; Occupancy and energy −0.20 pp; Other SG&A ~0.00 pp; FY2025 1.02%

claims.claim: Promotion mix: more sales sold on promotion at a lower margin, the largest gross-margin step
E-commerce: fulfillment net of fees rose from 0.4% to 1.2% of sales as orders tripled
Store labor: a real cost rise, but the third-smallest step
evidence: Store labor's share of the fall 13%

claims.claim: Promotion mix, shrink and private label together equal the 1.02 percentage-point fall in gross margin

slides.title: Growth has not protected profit: sales rose 6% in two years while operating income fell 68%

claims.claim: Sales kept growing in every year
Operating income fell by more than two-thirds
evidence: Operating income $M: FY2023 47.9; FY2024 33.4; FY2025 15.3

claims.claim: Each extra dollar of sales has earned less: the margin fell from 3.37% to 1.02%, so growth alone will not restore profit

slides.title: Three tests bound the plan: $29.8M more operating income by FY2028, $4.7M of it in FY2026

claims.claim: $29.8M a year more operating income for a 3.0% margin on FY2025 sales
evidence: 3.0% of FY2025 sales of $1,503.0M is $45.1M
Store exits shrink sales, so the dollar gap falls slightly
No sales growth is counted, at FY2025 prices
Close to double FY2025's $15.3M

claims.claim: $4.7M more in FY2026 than FY2025 to meet the lender's $20M covenant
evidence: Covenant: operating income of at least $20M in FY2026
Favors moves that pay within months
The draft plan's hours cut targets this test (2b)
The first test, and the nearest in time

claims.claim: $25M at most of one-time cost or capital over FY2026–FY2028
evidence: Rules out a large store refit program
Store closures with leases beyond 2027 need a board vote
Delivery stays in some form (owners)
Capital-light moves come first (5)

slides.title: Contents
In stores, the money is in shrink and the weakest sites, not in an across-the-board hours cut

claims.claim: Wages rose fast, but fewer hours per sale absorbed most of the rise
evidence: 0.3 pp rise in store labor as a share of sales, FY2023–25

claims.claim: An 8% hours cut would trade labor savings for higher shrink
evidence: Draft plan at risk · The cut the CFO and COO propose could lose most of its saving to shrink
0.5 pp rise in shrink while hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6%

claims.claim: Shrink is highest where hours are thinnest, so hours should move, not go
evidence: 3.1% shrink in the least-staffed quarter of stores, FY2025

claims.claim: Most of the nine loss-making stores can close as their leases end
evidence: 6 of the nine have leases ending by end-2027

slides.title: 2a: Wages rose 9.4% in two years, but fewer hours per sale held labor's rise to 0.3 percentage points of sales

claims.claim: 9.4% rise in the average hourly wage including benefits
evidence: From $16.80 to $18.38 an hour, FY2023 to FY2025
Minimum wage and a tight labor market (CFO and COO)
The minimum wage rises another 4% in 2027

claims.claim: −6% change in labor hours per $1,000 of sales
evidence: From 7.02 to 6.60 hours
Saved about $11.6M of store labor in FY2025
Shrink climbed over the same years (2c)

claims.claim: 0.3 pp rise in store labor as a share of sales
evidence: From 11.8% to 12.1% of sales
13% of the 2.35 percentage-point margin fall
Smaller than promotions, shrink or e-commerce

claims.claim: Wages are a headwind to manage, not the cause to fix first

slides.title: 2b: An 8% hours cut could hand back about $10.0M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink

claims.claim: $14.5M − $10.05M = $4.5M net saving a year, before any cost of longer checkout waits or stock-outs
evidence: $14.5M a year: the CFO and COO's estimate for an 8% cut in scheduled hours (8% of $181.9M store labor)
$10.05M a year of higher shrink: the FY2023–25 link (6% fewer hours per sale, 0.5 pp more shrink) scaled to 8%

claims.claim: On this estimate, the draft plan leaves FY2026 operating income near $19.8M, below the $20M covenant
The estimate assumes shrink keeps responding to hours as it did in FY2023–25
evidence: All of the 0.5 percentage-point shrink rise came from fewer hours per $1,000 of sales: an upper bound, since theft is 35% of shrink
Shrink rises in proportion to hours cut; the cut lands evenly on all stores, including the least-staffed
Sales held at FY2025 level; lost sales from service are not counted and would cut the net further

slides.title: 2c: The least-staffed stores lose 3.1% of sales to shrink, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: 35% more shrink per dollar of sales in the least-staffed quarter than in the best-staffed
evidence: Shrink % of sales FY2025: Q1 fewest hours 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Q4 most hours 2.3%
Q1: managers say rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
Q3 to Q4: extra hours buy only 0.1 percentage points less shrink

claims.claim: Move hours from Q4 stores to Q1 and Q2 stores instead of cutting them everywhere

slides.title: 2c: Most shrink is produce waste and receiving errors, the losses that skipped checks cause

claims.claim: Hours protect what customers come for
evidence: Composition of shrink FY2025: Fresh and produce waste 45%; Theft 35%; Administrative and receiving errors 20%
Customers: 58% name fresh produce as a top reason to shop at Harlow

claims.claim: Waste: the largest part, and the one rotation prevents
evidence: Stock not rotated goes off the shelf
Rotation is skipped first on busy days

claims.claim: Errors: receiving checks are the other task managers say they skip
evidence: Deliveries not checked at the door
Fixed by staffed receiving slots

claims.claim: Theft: the one part that staffing alone may not fix
evidence: Hours help less here
Needs its own controls

slides.title: 2c: Moving hours to the least-staffed stores, not cutting them, could take about $4.2M a year out of shrink

claims.claim: 0.3 pp × $1,414.5M = $4.2M a year of operating income from lower shrink
evidence: 0.3 pp of sales: fleet shrink of 2.6% above the 2.3% the best-staffed quarter already runs
$1,414.5M FY2028 sales at FY2025 prices, after the nine store exits (2d)

claims.claim: The target is a level a quarter of the stores already reach
evidence: Fleet shrink falls to 2.3% of sales, still above FY2023's 2.1%
Hours move from Q4 stores to Q1 and Q2 stores on busy days; total hours and labor cost stay flat
Produce rotation and receiving checks become fixed tasks in every schedule
Sales of $1,414.5M are FY2025 sales less the 75% of the nine stores' sales that would not transfer

slides.title: 2d: Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year, as a quarter of their sales moves to nearby stores

claims.claim: $3.1M + $3.5M = $6.6M a year of operating income from exiting all nine
evidence: $3.1M four-wall EBITDA loss of the nine stores removed (FY2025)
$3.5M contribution on sales that move: $118.0M × 25% moving × 12% contribution (past closures)

claims.claim: Past closures set the transfer rate; the estimate errs low
evidence: 25% of the nine stores' sales move to a nearby Harlow store, as in past closures, at 12% contribution
Allocated overheads are not saved and depreciation savings are not counted
Harlow sales fall by $88.5M, which the margin math in section 5 includes
Nine of 58 stores have negative four-wall EBITDA; the other 49 are not touched

slides.title: 2d: Most store exits need no board vote: six leases end by 2027, and the other three cost $7.5M to leave

claims.claim: Leases ending by end-2027: Start here / No exit cost and no vote: two-thirds of the store gain
evidence: 6 stores; One-time exit cost: None: leave at lease end; $4.4M operating income a year; Management; at each lease end in FY2027
$6.6M ÷ 9 × 6 = $4.4M a year from the six, at an even split

claims.claim: Leases running beyond 2027: Decide once the six show the real sales transfer
evidence: 3 stores; $7.5M one-time exit cost; $2.2M operating income a year; Board vote; payback about 3.4 years

slides.title: Contents
Promotions are the largest gross-margin leak, and resetting them is the largest single move in the plan

claims.claim: Promotions caused most of the gross-margin decline, and vendors pay less of them
evidence: 29% of FY2025 sales were on promotion, up from 24% in FY2023

claims.claim: The ValuMart threat is local, so promotions can go back to the FY2023 mix elsewhere
evidence: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money after counting extra units

claims.claim: Private label is still the best margin lever on the shelf
evidence: 12 pp more gross margin than national brands

slides.title: 3a: Promotion mix alone explains more than two-thirds of the gross-margin decline

claims.claim: 69% of the 1.02 percentage-point gross-margin fall came from the shift to promotional sales
evidence: Chart: FY2023 26.04%; Promotion mix −0.70 pp; Shrink −0.50 pp; Private label +0.18 pp; FY2025 25.02%
Promotion mix: 5 percentage points more of sales sold at 14 percentage points less margin
Shrink: the part tied to store hours (section 2)
Private label: a 1.5 percentage-point share gain offset about a quarter of the promotion loss

claims.claim: The three drivers add up to the full gross-margin change; the briefing pack gives no other driver

slides.title: 3a: Harlow promoted more while vendors paid less of the cost

claims.claim: Promotional sales rose every year
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional sales % of sales: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Vendors now fund less than half of the markdowns
evidence: −9 pp
Vendor funding % of promotional markdowns: FY2023 55%; FY2025 46%

claims.claim: Every event that stays should carry vendor funding: the fall to 46% is a negotiation, not a market fact

slides.title: 3b: The ValuMart threat is local, yet network-wide promotions have not improved Harlow's price image

claims.claim: Stores near a new ValuMart lose sales; the rest still grow
evidence: Comparable sales FY2025: Within three miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; Other Harlow stores +1.1%
ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas since 2023; the pack does not say how many Harlow stores sit within three miles of one

claims.claim: More shoppers find Harlow expensive, despite deeper promotions
evidence: +8 pp
Customers saying Harlow is more expensive: FY2023 33%; FY2025 41%
Price survey of 3,100 customers

slides.title: 3b: The evidence that promotions work counts sales, not profit, and ignores where the stores are

claims.claim: It counts sales, not profit
evidence: Deepest-promotion stores grew comparable sales 1.8%, against 0.2% for the rest
Promotional sales earn 14 percentage points less margin than regular-price sales
38% of FY2025 events lost money even after counting the extra units

claims.claim: It is not like for like
evidence: It does not separate stores near a new ValuMart from the rest
Stores near ValuMart run −4.2% comparable sales, so where depth sits matters most
A store-matched test of event profit would settle it in a quarter

claims.claim: Customers come for fresh and convenience
evidence: 58% name fresh produce and 44% convenience as top reasons to shop Harlow
41% now say Harlow is more expensive, up from 33% despite more promotions
Everyday value such as private label fits that better than event depth

claims.claim: Keep promotional depth where ValuMart is close, and judge every other event on profit, not sales

slides.title: 3b: Returning promotions to the FY2023 mix would add about $9.9M a year, mostly by dropping money-losing events

claims.claim: 5 pp × 14 pp × $1,414.5M = $9.9M a year of operating income
evidence: 5 pp of sales moved off promotion: from 29% back to FY2023's 24%
14 pp more gross margin on regular-price sales than on promotional sales
$1,414.5M FY2028 sales at FY2025 prices, after the nine store exits

claims.claim: The cut is smaller than the share of events that lose money
evidence: The cut removes about a sixth (17%) of promotional sales, against the 38% of events that lost money
Dropped events lost money after counting their extra units, so their lost volume is not counted
Promotional depth stays in ValuMart trade areas; the cuts fall on the other stores
Vendor funding stays at 46% of markdowns; any recovery toward 55% is upside

slides.title: 3c: Keeping private label's FY2023–25 pace would add about $3.8M a year by FY2028

claims.claim: $3.8M operating income by FY2028
evidence: 18.5% + 2.2 pp = 20.7% share of sales in FY2028; three more years at the FY2023–25 pace of 0.75 pp a year
2.25 pp of share × 12 pp margin premium × $1,414.5M sales

claims.claim: Margin and price image in one move
evidence: Margin: each point of share moved to private label earns 12 percentage points more
Price image: an own-brand alternative answers the 41% who say Harlow is more expensive

slides.title: Contents
E-commerce loses money, but repricing delivery cuts the loss while keeping the service the owners want

claims.claim: Counted in full, e-commerce loses money, most of it on home delivery
evidence: −$12.3 per home delivery after crediting the new sales it brings, FY2025

claims.claim: Customers accept higher delivery fees, and many switch to click-and-collect
evidence: Tested, not assumed · The fee test ran in 4 stores for 10 weeks; the rollout needs no new capability
−2% change in e-commerce sales when the delivery fee rose to $7.99

slides.title: 4a: Fulfillment cost grew 3.5 times in two years, faster than orders, as home delivery took a larger share

claims.claim: 3.5x growth in fulfillment cost, against 2.9 times the orders
evidence: E-commerce fulfillment $M: FY2023 5.2; FY2024 10.9; FY2025 18.1
Mix: home delivery rose from 45% to 58% of orders
Cost: third-party cost per delivery rose from $12.90 to $13.80
Fees: the fee collected per delivery fell from $3.40 to $3.10, as delivery is free above $75 against a $96 basket

slides.title: 4a: Each home delivery loses about $12 even after crediting the new sales it brings

claims.claim: −$12.3 per home delivery, FY2025
evidence: $5.76 contribution: $96 basket × 30% new × 20 cents
Less $7.40 picking and $13.80 delivery
Plus only $3.10 of fee collected

claims.claim: −$1.6 per click-and-collect order, FY2025
evidence: No third-party delivery cost
Close to break-even
Each order moved from delivery saves $10.70

claims.claim: −$9.04 per home delivery at the tested fee
evidence: Fee collected rises to $6.40
Still a loss per delivery
Next lever: the 2026 delivery contract

slides.title: 4a: Counted in full, e-commerce costs Harlow about $10.4M a year, not the profit its team reports

claims.claim: $127.8M × 30% × 20% − $18.1M = −$10.4M a year: what e-commerce does to operating income
evidence: $127.8M e-commerce sales, FY2025 (1,331k orders × $96)
30% of it new to Harlow: 70% would otherwise be bought in store (survey, n = 2,300)
20% contribution per new dollar before fulfillment (finance)
$18.1M fulfillment, including delivery net of fees

claims.claim: The team's 6.1% margin leaves out two things
evidence: It leaves out third-party delivery, which finance books in fulfillment
It treats every online sale as new; at 6.1% it reports about $7.8M of profit
Sales that moved from stores earn what they would have earned in store
E-commerce would break even only if about 71% of its sales were new, against 30% in the survey

slides.title: 4b: Customers accepted higher delivery fees: the test lost 2% of e-commerce sales and doubled the fee per delivery

claims.claim: 2.1x the fee collected per delivery: $6.40, against $3.10 in FY2025
evidence: Change during the fee test (4 stores, 10 weeks, late FY2025; fee $7.99, free delivery above $100): Delivered orders −9%; Click-and-collect orders +14%; E-commerce sales −2%
Delivered: 9% fewer of the orders that lose the most
Click-and-collect: 14% more orders in the channel that nearly breaks even
Sales: a small loss for a large cut in cost per order

claims.claim: Roll the tested fee and threshold out to all 58 stores in the first quarter

slides.title: 4b: Rolling the tested fees out to every store would recover about $2.8M a year and keep delivery for those who pay

claims.claim: $18.1M − $15.1M − $0.2M = $2.8M a year of operating income
evidence: $18.1M fulfillment net of fees, FY2025
$15.1M after the test response: 9% fewer deliveries, 14% more collections, $6.40 fee
$0.2M contribution lost on the 2% of sales that go (new sales only)

claims.claim: The test response holds in every store
evidence: The 4-store, 10-week test response holds in all 58 stores
Picking ($7.40) and delivery ($13.80) cost per order stay at FY2025 levels
Lost sales lose 20 cents of contribution only on the 30% that is new to Harlow
The provider's proposed 3% rate rise is refused at the 2026 renewal; accepting it costs about $0.3M a year

slides.title: Contents
Five moves lift the margin to 3.0% of sales by FY2028, and the promotions reset is the largest

claims.claim: 3.02% operating margin in FY2028 at FY2025 prices, against the 3.0% target
evidence: Chart: FY2025 15.3; Promotions reset +9.90; Private label +3.82; Shrink +4.24; Delivery fees +2.83; Store exits +6.64; FY2028 42.74 ($M)

claims.claim: Promotions reset: about a third of the gain, and it needs no capital
Store exits: six at lease end; three need a vote and $7.5M
At risk: the 2027 wage rise could cost up to $7.3M (section 5)

slides.title: The draft plan could miss the lender's covenant, because it cuts a cost that did not cause the decline

claims.claim: Store labor — The decisive difference / Cutting hours treats the smallest cause and feeds the second-largest, shrink
evidence: Draft plan: Cut hours 8% in every store; Recommended plan: Move hours to understaffed stores

claims.claim: Shrink: Protects fresh produce
evidence: Draft: Likely to rise with fewer hours; Recommended: Down to 2.3% of sales

claims.claim: Promotions: Largest single move
evidence: Draft: Not addressed; Recommended: Back to the FY2023 mix

claims.claim: E-commerce: Delivery stays
evidence: Draft: Frozen; still losing $10.4M a year; Recommended: Tested delivery fees everywhere

claims.claim: Stores: Three by board vote
evidence: Draft: Not addressed; Recommended: Nine exits, six at lease end

claims.claim: Operating income before the wage rise: Draft misses $20M
evidence: Draft $19.8M; Recommended About $42.7M by FY2028
$15.3M FY2025 operating income + $4.5M net hours saving after shrink (2b) = $19.8M draft-plan operating income, all else flat

slides.title: Promotions, delivery fees and store hours come first: they are fast, need no capital and cover the covenant

claims.claim: The covenant is the nearest test
evidence: $4.7M FY2026 needs this much more operating income than FY2025

claims.claim: No capital
evidence: All three run on pricing, the promotion calendar and schedules; the budget is untouched

claims.claim: Already proven or in our control
evidence: Fees were tested in 4 stores; event profit is already measured

claims.claim: Moves positioned by speed and size: Start now (Promotions reset, Store hours and shrink, Delivery fees); Plan now, lands later (Six store exits, Private label); Decide on evidence (Three store exits)
evidence: Positions are judged; sizes follow the run-rate estimates in sections 2–4. At full run-rate the three first moves are worth about 3.6 times the $4.7M covenant need

slides.title: Three waves take the plan from no-capital moves in the first quarter to store exits in FY2027

claims.claim: Wave 1 decides the covenant; waves 2 and 3 decide the 3.0% target
evidence: Promotions reset: Drop money-losing events; vendor talks
Delivery fees: Tested fees, all stores
Store hours and shrink: Move hours; fixed rotation tasks
Private label: New ranges at the FY2023–25 pace
Six store exits: At each lease end
Three store exits: Board vote, then exit

slides.title: 5a: A promotions reset targets money-losing events and keeps depth where ValuMart competes

claims.claim: Return promotional sales to the FY2023 share of 24% without losing ValuMart-area traffic
evidence: $9.9M a year by FY2028 (3b)

claims.claim: Key actions: Diagnose, Cut, Fund
evidence: Rank every FY2025 event by profit after extra units
Tag stores within three miles of a ValuMart
Drop money-losing events outside ValuMart areas first

Offer free click-and-collect first at online checkout
Refuse the proposed 3% rate rise at the 2026 renewal; tender if needed
Weekly: deliveries, collections and e-commerce sales against the test

evidence: $4.2M a year (2c)

slides.title: Two reserve moves worth about $6.5M would cover most of the 2027 wage rise, even if it reaches every wage

claims.claim: $2.8M + $3.6M = $6.5M a year from the two reserves ÷ $7.3M = 89% of that wage risk covered
evidence: $2.8M shrink down to FY2023's 2.1% of sales instead of 2.3%
$3.6M 8% fewer hours in the best-staffed quarter, once shrink holds
$7.3M upper bound of the 2027 wage rise: 4% on all store labor

claims.claim: The wage figure is an upper bound; the reserves are held back on purpose
evidence: Many staff already earn above the minimum, so the real cost of the 4% rise is likely lower
No price rise recovers wage costs; all figures at FY2025 prices
Q4 stores carry a quarter of store labor; their cut waits until shrink holds at 2.3%
Vendor funding back toward 55% and depreciation saved on exited stores are further upside, not sized

claims.claim: ValuMart: Traffic falls as promotions are cut — Highest risk
evidence: Early signal: Comparable sales in ValuMart-area stores; Response: Depth stays there; cuts fall elsewhere; Owner: Chief merchant
Stores near a new ValuMart already run −4.2% comparable sales

claims.claim: Delivery customers: Customers leave over the new fee
evidence: Early signal: E-commerce sales down more than the test's 2%; Response: Adjust the threshold; promote collection; Owner: Head of e-commerce; Weekly tracking

claims.claim: Shrink: Shrink does not fall in Q1 stores
evidence: Early signal: Monthly shrink by store; Response: Check task compliance; hold Q4 hours; Owner: COO; Reserve stays unused

claims.claim: Wages: The 2027 rise reaches every wage
evidence: Early signal: 2027 wage settlement; Response: Use the reserves (section 5); Owner: CFO; Up to $7.3M

claims.claim: Store exits: Less sales move than in past closures
evidence: Early signal: Receiving-store sales after each exit; Response: Decide the last three on the real rate; Owner: CEO; Before the vote

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Approve the five-move plan and replace the 8% hours cut: return promotions to the FY2023 mix outside ValuMart areas and grow private label; move store hours instead of cutting them; keep e-commerce but charge for delivery (roll out the tested $7.99 fee and $100 threshold); exit the nine loss-making stores (six at lease end, three by board vote). First: promotions, delivery fees and store hours, which need no capital.

alternatives_considered.option: Draft plan: cut hours 8% in every store (CFO and COO proposal)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: an 8% hours cut could hand back about $10.0M of its $14.5M saving through higher shrink; leaves FY2026 operating income near $19.8M, below the $20M covenant; "cuts a cost that did not cause the decline". Replaced by moving hours to understaffed stores; an 8% cut in Q4 hours is held as a reserve only once shrink holds at 2.3%.
Left out: flat at 4.7% of sales in FY2023 and FY2025; the pack holds no overhead data to size a cut.
Left out: 41% already say Harlow is more expensive, and ValuMart is opening nearby.
Left out: the owners want delivery kept in some form; repricing it is in the plan instead (4b). Listed as out of scope in the brief.

alternatives_considered.option: Exit the three loss-making stores with leases beyond 2027
alternatives_considered.treatment: Deferred: $7.5M exit cost, board vote, payback about 3.4 years; decide once the six show the real sales transfer.

alternatives_considered.option: Accept the delivery provider's proposed 3% rate rise
alternatives_considered.treatment: Refuse at the 2026 renewal; tender if needed; accepting it costs about $0.3M a year.

alternatives_considered.option: Refinancing the covenant; spending beyond the $25M budget
alternatives_considered.treatment: Out of scope per the brief.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All moves are sized at FY2025 prices and volumes; no sales growth is counted; FY2026 is treated as the first plan year
Hours-cut estimate assumes shrink keeps responding to hours as it did in FY2023–25; all of the 0.5 pp shrink rise attributed to fewer hours is an upper bound, since theft is 35% of shrink
Lost sales from service (checkout waits, stock-outs) are not counted
Shrink target 2.3% is a planning choice: the best-staffed quarter's FY2025 level; total hours and labor cost stay flat
25% of the nine stores' sales move to nearby Harlow stores, as in past closures, at 12% contribution; allocated overheads not saved and depreciation savings not counted; the estimate errs low
$4.4M from the six exits assumes an even split of the $6.6M
Promotional share target 24% (FY2023 mix) is a planning choice; dropped events' lost volume not counted; vendor funding stays at 46%, any recovery toward 55% is upside
Private-label pace for three more years at the FY2023–25 pace is a planning choice
The 4-store, 10-week fee test response holds in all 58 stores; picking and delivery cost per order stay at FY2025 levels
30% of e-commerce sales are new to Harlow (survey of 2,300); 20% contribution per new dollar (finance estimate)
The provider's proposed 3% rate rise is refused at the 2026 renewal
2027 wage rise could cost up to $7.3M (upper bound: 4% on all store labor); many staff already earn above the minimum, so real cost likely lower; no price rise recovers wage costs
With full wage rise and reserves, the FY2028 margin is 2.96%, just under 3.0%

Risks: ValuMart traffic response to fewer promotions (highest risk); delivery customers leaving over the new fee; shrink not falling in Q1 stores; wage rise reaching every wage; less sales transfer after exits
Open questions: promotional depth near ValuMart; delivery contract rate; reach of the 2027 wage rise; service after hours move; vendor funding
The pack does not say how many Harlow stores sit within three miles of a ValuMart; the pack holds no overhead data
Matrix positions on slide 35 are judged

Move hours to Q1 and Q2 stores; report shrink by store monthly — COO — First quarter
Confirm lease dates for the six exits; prepare the vote on the other three — CEO and CFO — Next board meeting
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text with no images. I rounded the chart series values (bridge steps, shares) to the units the slides use, without changing them. Waterfall charts came as 'base' and value series, and I transcribed the step values only. The positions on the slide 35 bubble matrix came from the text labels, so their spatial layout may not be exact. Slide 3's headline became the governing thought, and its five numbered points plus sub-bullets are in the executive summary. The deck gives two different figures for the private-label pace: 0.75 pp a year on slide 24 and 0.7 pp on slide 48. I left both as written.
